source_name: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention
text: Introducing the most common food allergens in the first year of life, when infants show signs of readiness (usually around 6 months, not before 4 months), has been shown to reduce the risk of developing food allergy. Well-cooked whole egg and peanut should be introduced soon after starting solids.

source_name: BSACI Early Introduction of Food Allergens
text: Early introduction of allergenic foods, rather than avoidance, is now recommended as a strategy to reduce the risk of food allergy developing in infancy, in line with current international consensus.
Deliberately delaying the introduction of allergenic solids beyond 6 months of age is not recommended and may increase the risk of food allergy and eczema.
Complementary foods should be introduced at 6 months of age while continuing to breastfeed, gradually increasing food quantity and variety as the infant grows.

source_name: ASCIA Signs and Symptoms of Allergic Reactions
text: Signs of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) include difficulty breathing, swelling of the tongue, swelling or tightness in the throat, wheeze or persistent cough, and persistent dizziness. This requires immediate emergency treatment.

source_name: ASCIA Position Statement: Food Allergen Starter Packs for Infants
text: Infant formula based on alternative proteins, including goat milk, sheep milk, rice, oat, pea, or coconut protein, is not recommended for food allergy prevention due to a lack of supporting evidence.

source_name: BSACI Early Introduction of Food Allergens
text: Allergenic foods should not be introduced before 4 months of age, as infants are not developmentally ready for solid foods and breast milk or formula should remain the primary source of nutrition.
Continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods is recommended for as long as the mother and child wish to continue, ideally up to two years of age or beyond.
